source_terms: The most effective testimonial commercials are those which show loyal users of your product testifying to its virtues – when they don't know they are being filmed.
The interviewer pretends to find fault with the product and the loyal user rises to its defense with far more conviction than if you simply asked him what he thought of it.
The more amateurish the performance, the more credible.
item.claim: The most effective testimonial commercials show loyal users testifying when they do not know they are being filmed, and the source describes a specific device for producing conviction: the interviewer attacks the product and the user rises to its defence, which he says produces far more conviction than asking what the user thinks. He states the selection rule that follows — avoid users who would give so polished a performance that viewers would take them for professional actors, because the more amateurish the performance the more credible it is. His supporting case is a French campaign that cast an eighty-year-old laundress as its heroine; she became recognised by three in four people in France and the product is reported to have moved from fourth to second in sales.

mechanism.text: Credibility comes from the speaker appearing not to be performing for the advertiser. Defending the product against an attack, and doing it clumsily, are both signals that the speech is the speaker's own.

caveats.text: the mechanism is a claim about how sincerity is read, and the technique described — filming people who do not know they are being filmed, with an actor posing as a dealer — is a staged authenticity, which the source does not comment on

source_terms: If you include a testimonial in your copy, you make it more credible. Readers find the endorsements of fellow consumers more persuasive than the puffery of anonymous copywriters.

source_terms: The Law of Credentials
The crucial ingredient in the success of any brand is its claim to authenticity.
Credentials are the collateral you put up to guarantee the performance of your brand.
item.claim: Law 6. The authors start from customer disbelief: prospects are suspicious and discount most product claims. They argue one claim takes precedence over all others because it makes the others credible — the claim to authenticity, to being the real thing. Benefit claims made without credentials are, on their account, generally ignored, because every competitor makes the same sort of claim; the same benefit claims attached to a credential carry much more weight. They extend the point to buyer behaviour generally with the empty-restaurant observation: people prefer to wait for a table where there is a queue rather than eat in an empty room.

mechanism.text: Credentials work as collateral. A claim about performance is unverifiable at the point of choice, so the prospect looks for something that stands behind it; where a brand supplies that, the prospect will believe almost anything else it says. Absent it, benefit claims fall into the undifferentiated mass that provokes "that's what they all say".

scope.conditions: wherever prospects cannot verify a product claim before buying

caveats.text: 'the crucial ingredient in the success of any brand' is a universal claim demonstrated by one advertising line (Coca-Cola's 'the real thing') and two consulting cases of the authors' own

item.question: Ogilvy states the celebrity-testimonial problem three times in three chapters with three different framings. Give the three, and state the single exception that survives in all of them.

source_terms: any light positioned within the family of angles will produce a direct reflection

item.claim: Whether a direct reflection appears is decided entirely by whether the light sits inside the family of angles. A light inside it produces one; a light outside it does not light a mirror-like subject at all as far as the camera is concerned. To see direct reflection across most of a mirror-like surface, the source must be large enough to fill the family; to see none, both camera and light must be placed so the source falls outside it.

item.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
item.question: Freeman is careful to distinguish "close" from "close-up". What is the difference in his terms, and what common assumption about equipment does he remove?
item.answer: Close-up, he says, is to do with magnification of small things. Close is a sense of being right up against the subject, shooting from nearer than most people would consider normal and possibly nearer than feels comfortable. The assumption he removes is that close means a wide-angle lens: he says close viewpoints do not always mean wide-angle lenses, and his own example was shot at close to normal, 48mm, with tight framing doing the work instead. He also separates the practical reasons for being close — no room to stand back, obstructions such as telegraph lines forcing an architectural photographer nearer — from the expressive one, and only the expressive one carries his claim about a personal and emotional connection.
item.support: CLOSE, converted-PDF page 110. The close/close-up distinction, the 48mm figure and the separation of practical from expressive reasons are all stated there.
confounders: the widespread assumption that a close viewpoint requires a wide-angle lens, which he contradicts with his own focal length
reading 'close' as macro or detail work, which is exactly the confusion he is guarding against
assuming the emotional connection comes from the lens rather than from the physical distance and the subject's eye level

item.question: A producer is scheduling a one-day shoot with an infant. What does this source record as standard practice, what is the reason, and what must not be inferred from it?
item.answer: That a full day may yield only about five seconds of usable footage, because the subject's state cannot be directed, and that consequently no baby shoot is booked with fewer than three infants standing by. The reason is that the performance cannot be directed, only waited for, so usable footage is a function of chance over time — adding interchangeable subjects multiplies the independent chances within the same booked day rather than extending the day. What must not be inferred: this is advice about photographing a live human infant and is evidence about nothing whatever concerning a generative model. Any binding from it stays a production candidate with a null target path.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Shoot the Picture' in the dark-field sequence
item.question: The edge highlights in a dark-field glass shot are far too small for an ordinary meter. What proxy does the book use, and why does it then insist on a bracket?
item.answer: The proxy is the light source itself. Because a pure direct reflection is as bright as the source that produces it, the reflections may be too small to read but the large source is not: place the meter close enough to read the source alone, read the EDGE of the source because that is the part illuminating the glass, and open two stops to place it near white rather than at the meter's assumed 18% grey. The bracket is required because that exposure is only correct if the highlight on the glass is a perfect un-polarized direct reflection, and in practice there is no realistic chance of it being both. So the authors treat that value as a theoretical starting point and try one, two and three stops more. They also note that a correct instrument would be a spot meter of much less than one degree, that few photographers own one, and that bracketing with a conventional meter is an acceptably close approximation — an explicit substitution of procedure for instrument.
item.support: Ch. 7, the 'Shoot the Picture' step of the dark-field sequence. The source-brightness fact and the dimming of polarized reflection are both chapter-3 material and already live Canon.

item.question: Compare a small bright highlight and a large dim one on the surface of a glass. What does the book say each does for the viewer, and what sets the difference in practice?
item.answer: They do opposite jobs. The tiny bright spots are distracting at the least and meaningless at best: they are too small and too bright to tell the viewer anything about surface detail or texture. A large highlight informs — it serves the constructive purpose of saying how the glass surface looks and feels. In practice the difference is set by how much of the relevant family of angles is filled with light, and, with a diffusion sheet, by the distance from the lamp head to the sheet: close in, only the centre of the sheet lights and the highlight is small and bright; pulled back, the whole sheet lights and reflects as a larger highlight. The authors add that the larger highlight should usually be kept dimmer, because a brightly lit whole sheet reflects as an obvious hard-edged rectangle that advertises a studio light and costs the scene its reality — and that strips of black tape on the sheet can make the reflection read as a window instead.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Defining the Surface of Glassware', including the two matched highlight frames and the taped diffusion sheet.
confounders: assuming brighter highlights read as more premium or more glossy
attributing the difference to the size of the source alone, ignoring the lamp-to-diffuser distance
missing that the source deliberately makes the large highlight dimmer, not brighter

item.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
item.source_locator: Ch. "Getting close", sub-heading "Get close. And then get closer." (spine 12)
item.question: A photographer says they will shoot from further back and crop in afterwards to get the same tight frame. On Carroll's account, what have they lost, and what is his stated reason?
item.answer: They have lost the thing he says the picture actually carries. Carroll raises this exact substitution and rejects it: cropping is a fine tuner, not a way to fundamentally alter an image. His reason is relational rather than optical — the photographer's physical exposure to the subject is part of what the picture means. He says of the photographer in his example that it matters that he puts himself in the line of fire, and that if he did not, the pictures would lose their humour and start to feel underhand. So the loss is not resolution; it is the fact of the encounter. Note the scope: he is talking about candid work with people, and elsewhere he recommends a long lens precisely where approach is impossible.
item.support: Getting close spread: nothing kills an image more than keeping your distance; think of cropping as a fine tuner rather than a way of fundamentally altering your image; it's important that the photographer puts himself in the line of fire, or the pictures would feel underhand.
confounders: answering in terms of image quality, resolution or lens sharpness — Carroll's reason is not technical
assuming he forbids cropping; he permits it as a fine tuner
generalising the rule to all subjects; his scope is subjects that could have been approached
